constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: The desert valley had opened up in a split second. Elias was checking his maps when the IED detonated, a wall of heat and shrapnel that turned the morning quiet into a roaring, disorienting storm. Through the smoke, he remembered the frantic grip of his sergeant hauling him behind a burning Humvee, the sudden, crushing weight of another soldier dropping beside him, the deafening cracks of incoming fire that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The chaos never resolved into a clear sequence; the blast had shattered the timeline, leaving him with only jagged fragments. Now, when he tries to walk his wife through what he survived, he loses the thread after the first minute, his voice tightening as he admits he simply cannot explain it clearly. The terror that floods back when he pieces those fragments together feels exactly as it did in the valley, a visceral wave that still stops his heart. Those fractured recollections quickly became unbearable, which is why Elias began filling his home with blaring television and thumping bass, desperate to drown out the silence before the images could return. He found himself constantly scanning his own mind for any slip toward madness, treating every stray worry like a crack in his sanity. The more he tried to outrun the memories by turning up the volume, the more his physiology stayed locked in the past. He began jolting awake the moment a hand brushed his shoulder, his breath catching in alarm whenever a colleague at the council chamber accidentally grazed his arm while passing a dossier. Even when the chamber was empty and the lights were dimmed, he could not convince himself that the danger had passed. Elias had come to believe that his own body was actively betraying him, keeping him in a state of perpetual combat readiness long after he had hung up his uniform. Because he trusted his physiology over logic, he dismissed his wife's reassurances that the city streets were secure, his skepticism hardening into a rigid inability to accept any safety. The constant feeling that the world remained an unsafe place pushed him to stand at the perimeter of every town hall, eyes darting across the crowd, scanning for threats that never materialized. The relentless startle responses and chronic inability to settle into sleep convinced him that his body was an unreliable asset and that the world outside was fundamentally hostile. Each time his nerves flared, however, the alarm only sharpened his focus on the unexplained gaps in his combat narrative, driving him back to the terrifying fragments he desperately wanted to forget. To quiet the rising dread, Elias avoided physical contact entirely, declining handshakes at public forums and pulling his sleeves down over his wrists during committee meetings. This deliberate isolation, however, only left his mind unanchored, allowing the fragmented combat scenes to surface more frequently during his lonely evenings. The constant noise and mental vigilance only hardened his belief that his body was an unreliable asset and that the world outside was fundamentally hostile. Over months, the habit of monitoring his own thoughts for impending breakdowns and keeping the television at maximum volume only widened the gaps in his recall and deepened his distrust of his own reactions. The cycle tightened relentlessly through the autumn council sessions. Every time a constituent reached out to offer support, Elias flinched and stepped back, fearing the touch would trigger the same paralysis he felt under fire. The avoidance that once protected him now left him isolated in his office, staring at blank policy briefs while his pulse raced. Constituents began noticing his withdrawn demeanor, and his reputation for steady leadership eroded into whispers of instability. He finally booked an appointment after a constituent collapsed during a public rally, the sudden rush of hands and shouts pushing him over the edge. He does not know if he can ever trust his own mind again, but he is desperate to stop the terror from dictating his days.
